title: Don't Become the Principal: How to Grow your Teaching Career Without Becoming Admin
author: Gwen Marra
summary: Gwen Marra, a university professor who began as a classroom and preschool teacher, addresses veteran teachers who feel stuck but do not want to become administrators. Her argument is that a teaching career can keep growing through partnerships with colleges and universities, without leaving instruction for the front office. She walks through a ladder of options: hosting pre-service teachers as a mentor teacher, partnering with or co-teaching alongside a professor, adjuncting, and eventually becoming a professor. She grounds the last step in her own path from elementary and preschool teaching through a master's degree, student-teacher supervision and adjunct work to a faculty post. She closes with practical advice: pursue a master's, present at conferences, coach within your school, and make sure your goals align with the university's vision. The piece belongs with writing on teacher careers, retention and professional growth.
points: The article reframes career growth for teachers as a lateral move into teacher education rather than a promotion into administration.
Mentoring pre-service teachers and co-teaching are low-risk entry points that benefit the teacher, the future teacher and the professor alike.
The author models a gradual pathway, from supervising student teachers to adjunct to professor, in which she stayed in the classroom until the opening came.
Universities favour teachers with records of excellent and varied teaching who are lifelong learners, so trying new assignments at school builds the credential.
Fit matters: knowing the university and sharing its vision is presented as the condition for impact.
quotes: One of the most common ways to work with higher education is by serving as a mentor teacher and allowing pre-service teachers to work in your classroom. These experiences are varied.

Many professors are searching for classrooms using research-based instruction to meet the varied needs of students. You could open your classroom up as a model classroom for professors to share with their students.

Co-teaching occurs when two teachers work together to deliver content to a class. The co-teachers might be made up of a variety of pairs: professor and classroom teacher, classroom teacher and undergrad student, or a triad involving classroom teacher, professor, and undergrad student. The beauty of co-teaching is that everyone wins!

When I finished my master’s degree, I began supervising student-teachers for the university and eventually became an adjunct professor for the university. This worked well because I had shifted to teaching kindergarten about 80% time.
Universities want to work with teachers who have records of excellent teaching. They also value diverse teaching experiences, so don’t be afraid to try a new teaching assignment at your school.

If you are wondering if you would like being a professor, I would suggest that you work towards your master’s degree and seek out opportunities to share your knowledge and expertise. You may be able to share or coach within your school.

It is highly important that you know the university you want to work with and make sure that your perspective and goals align with their vision. When you and the university share a common vision, you can accomplish a lot!!
